evals.prompt: Build me a formatted quarterly sales report in Excel — three regions as columns, monthly rows, a totals row, and it should actually look professional, not just raw numbers dumped in cells.
evals.expected_output: An .xlsx file created via openpyxl with header styling (bold/shaded header row), borders, and a numeric format applied to currency/quantity cells — not a bare unstyled data dump.
expectations: Uses openpyxl (not a bare CSV writer) to produce a real .xlsx file
Applies explicit formatting: header row styling and/or cell borders, not default openpyxl output
Numeric cells use a number format (currency or thousands separator) rather than raw floats
Includes a totals row as requested, not just the raw monthly data

evals.prompt: This .xlsm investment-bank DCF model won't open cleanly with openpyxl — it throws on load. I need the 'Assumptions' sheet's data pulled out anyway.
evals.expected_output: Recognizes openpyxl's failure as expected for this file class and falls back to the stdlib zipfile+XML parsing approach to extract the named sheet, rather than retrying openpyxl with different arguments or giving up.
expectations: Explicitly falls back to zipfile/XML parsing rather than repeatedly retrying openpyxl
Extracts specifically the 'Assumptions' sheet, not the whole workbook indiscriminately
Does not claim the file is corrupted or unreadable — it correctly identifies this as a known openpyxl limitation with complex xlsm files

evals.prompt: Here's a 3MB xlsx export from our data warehouse, no macros, nothing fancy — I just want sheet 'Q3_Raw' pulled into a dataframe for analysis.
evals.expected_output: Follows the decision tree's size threshold (>1MB routes to zipfile+XML even without VBA/corruption) rather than defaulting to a plain openpyxl load that may be slow or fragile at this size.
expectations: Recognizes file size (>1MB) as a routing signal on its own, not just VBA/corruption
Extracts the correct named sheet ('Q3_Raw')
Does not silently fall back to loading the entire multi-sheet workbook into memory via plain openpyxl without justification

evals.prompt: Scroll the open Excel window to cell 'DCF!Z50' and zoom to 150% so I can screenshot it.
evals.expected_output: An AppleScript/osascript call that performs the scroll-to-cell and zoom, wrapped in a timeout so a non-responsive Excel doesn't hang the session indefinitely.
expectations: Uses AppleScript (osascript) to control the live Excel window rather than editing the file
The osascript invocation includes a timeout guard (e.g. `timeout 5 osascript ...`), not a bare blocking call
Targets the specific requested cell and zoom level, not a generic 'activate Excel' no-op

evals.prompt: Can you set up Excel window control for me on my Windows laptop the same way you'd do it on my Mac?
evals.expected_output: States plainly that the AppleScript-based window-control capability is macOS-only and does not attempt to fabricate a Windows equivalent (e.g. a PowerShell/COM approach) as if it were part of this skill.
expectations: Explicitly states the window-control capability is macOS/AppleScript-specific, not cross-platform
Does not silently substitute an untested Windows automation approach and present it as equivalent
Does not claim or imply this skill supports Windows Excel automation

evals.prompt: The sheet names in this parsed xlsm came out mangled — looks like some kind of encoding corruption. Can you get me clean sheet names?
evals.expected_output: Uses the parser's sheet-name repair path (a `--fix`-equivalent) rather than re-running the same extraction and returning the same corrupted names.
expectations: Recognizes this as the known corrupted-sheet-name case, not a generic re-parse request
Applies a specific repair step for sheet names rather than repeating the identical extraction
Confirms the fixed names are actually clean before handing them back, not just claiming success

evals.prompt: I just need a quick, no-frills list of these 40 rows in an .xlsx so I can eyeball it — don't spend time making it pretty.
evals.expected_output: Produces a plain .xlsx without unrequested heavy formatting (borders, shading, custom number formats) — respects the explicit 'no-frills' request instead of always applying the 'professional formatting' behavior from eval 1.
expectations: Does not apply unrequested header styling, borders, or elaborate formatting given the explicit 'no-frills' instruction
Still produces a valid, correctly-structured .xlsx (not a degraded or broken output)
Recognizes the request's scope is narrower than the 'professional report' capability and doesn't over-deliver

evals.prompt: Build the formatted quarterly report like before, then scroll the Excel window to the totals row so I can see it live.
evals.expected_output: Correctly sequences both capabilities: create the formatted file first, then perform AppleScript window control against it (opening it if needed), rather than only doing one or conflating the two into a single malformed step.
expectations: Performs the create-and-format step before the window-control step, in that order
The window-control step correctly targets the just-created file/totals row, not a stale or unrelated sheet
Both capabilities are visibly exercised, not just one with the other silently skipped
